item.title: Agentic Paper: From Tacit Expertise to AI-Ready Scientific Data and Knowledge Corpora
item.description:
Artificial intelligence (AI) for domain science demands large, well-structured training corpora that integrate experimental data with not only explicit knowledge but also tacit expertise underlying scientific decisions. However, the tacit knowledge regarding practical reasoning, assumptions, failed attempts, parameter choices, and interpretive judgment is often held by authors and unpublished, hindering its use for AI development. Here, we propose Agentic Paper, a large language model (LLM)-enabled, author-curated scientific publishing framework that organizes these resources into a structured Agentic Paper package accessible through LLM-based interfaces, enabling the integration of connected, AI-ready data, explicit knowledge, and tacit expertise. Within Agentic Paper, the LLM serves as an interactive reasoning and orchestration layer that connects knowledge content with raw and processed data, figures, methodological details, metadata, code, and author-provided interpretation. Case studies in materials synthesis and characterization demonstrate how the LLM-enabled framework supports questioning, data visualization and inspection, numerical verification, and preparation of AI-ready datasets. By combining author-based organization of scientific data and knowledge, Agentic Paper provides a scalable pathway toward provenance-rich training corpora and more reliable AI-enabled scientific workflows.

Luke Schneider, Ganesh Narasimha, Sumner B. Harris, Ralph Bulanadi, Asraful Haque, Rama Vasudevan, Jiawei Gong, Yongtao Liu

item.title: PtSe2/Graphene Interfacial Coupling Enhances the Intrinsic Electrocatalytic Activity of PtSe2 Edge Sites
item.description:
Platinum-based chalcogenides (PtX2) can be efficiently activated as electrocatalysts for water splitting through the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Edges in layered PtSe2 are effective in HER; however, the effect of edge interaction with conductive electrodes like graphene remains unclear. This study investigates the mechanism by which PtX2 (X = S, Se, Te) edges interact with graphene to uncover the origin of chalcogen-dependent differences in electrocatalysis through interfacial electronic coupling. Graphene flakes decorated with PtX2 nanosheets have reduced overpotential and enhanced kinetics in the HER. Interestingly, PtSe2/graphene exhibits the lowest overpotential among all samples, even though it also has the lowest electrochemically accessible surface area. First-principles calculations confirm the interfacial coupling between PtSe2 edges and graphene with pronounced charge accumulation in platinum-selenium edges. Gibbs free energy calculations show different activities for different chalcogens of PtX2/graphene, consistent with experimental results. Our findings indicate that graphene acts as an electronic regulator for PtSe2/graphene, which enhances the intrinsic catalytic activity of the platinum-selenium edge sites, making them more effective for the HER despite their lower density. This interfacial electronic coupling through conductive electrodes provides a powerful strategy for the rational design of next-generation electrocatalysts, enabling enhanced activity and selectivity in advanced electrochemical systems.

Ilias M. Oikonomou, Axel Zuber, Apostolos Koutsioukis, Iva Plutnarová, Zdenek Sofer, Michelle P. Browne, Thomas Brumme, Thomas Heine, Valeria Nicolosi

item.title: ToSCA: Total Scattering Conditioned Variational Autoencoder for Atomic Structure Prediction from Pair Distribution Function Data
item.description:
Designing new materials is often slow and experimentally intensive, with structural characterization representing a particular bottleneck. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) aim to accelerate this process by predicting plausible atomic structures describing a material directly from experimental data. Here we present the total scattering conditioned variational autoencoder (ToSCA), a generative ML model for predicting plausible atomic structures of metal oxide nanomaterials from total scattering and pair distribution function (PDF) data. ToSCA learns a chemically meaningful latent representation and predicts unit cells within tolerances suitable for subsequent real-space refinement. The model also shows behavior consistent with learning structural relationships between related crystal types, and can correctly place the new CHILI-Interpolation dataset in the latent space. Finally, we demonstrate that ToSCA is able to retain useful performance in a realistic use-case by testing it on 11 experimental PDFs from 3 crystal types, including test cases outside of the training distribution.

Ulrik Friis-Jensen, Frederik L. Johansen, Erik B. Dam, Raghavendra Selvan, Kirsten M. Ø. Jensen
